chunks: Measuring motor or solenoid current. The question: How do you determine how much current a motor/solenoid is drawing?
To measure the current in a motor or solenoid, the usual method is a shunt: a very small resistor in the current path.
The current makes a small voltage across it, V equals I times R . An amplifier scales that voltage up so the microcontroller's ADC (its voltage-to-number converter) can read it.
The catch is that "current drawn" depends on where you measure, because a PWM drive chops the current into pulses.
Picture a ring road with a toll booth at the entrance. While the entrance gate is open, cars flow in and keep circling the ring.
When it shuts, the cars already on the ring keep circling. An entrance counter sees only cars coming through the gate. A counter on the ring sees them all.
The entrance counter is the supply shunt, and the ring counter is a shunt in series with the motor.
The orange shunt R hs sees the pulsed supply current; the blue shunt R ls sees the motor current only while Q1 conducts.
Neither sees the free-wheel current circulating through D1 and the motor.
To see it you put the shunt in series with the motor itself (in-line), at the cost of a switching common-mode voltage.
Shunt resistor: a precision resistor of a few milliohms. Its voltage drop measures current. Current-sense amplifier (CSA): an amplifier that scales up that small drop.
PWM and duty cycle ( D ): PWM switches the supply fully on and off very fast. The duty cycle is the fraction of each period it is on.
Free-wheel current: the current that keeps circulating through a diode across the motor (the flyback diode) when the switch is off.
Say the current is up to 20 amps and the shunt is 2 milliohms. At full current it drops 20 times 0. 002 equals 0. 04 volts, or 40 millivolts.
An amplifier with a gain of 75 turns 40 millivolts into 3. 0 volts. On a 12-bit (4096-step) ADC each count is about 5. 4 milliamps.
A separate trap: if the motor current is a smooth 4 amps at 50% duty, a bench supply shows only about 2 amps. That is the whole idea.
"Most commonly a milliohm-scale shunt resistor plus a current-sense amplifier into the ADC: 20 amps through 2 milliohms is 40 millivolts, gain 75 gives 3 volts.
Low-side is simple but only sees on-time current; high-side or in-line sees more but needs a high-common-mode amplifier.
Hall sensors give isolation, MOSFET R DS(on) sensing saves a part but drifts with temperature.
Because PWM chops the current I sample mid on-time or filter, and calibrate offset at zero current."
